title: Why Do You See STARS When You Rub Your Eyes? ✨
description:
You rub your eyes and the darkness fills with stars. No light got in: your eyeball just pocket-dialed your brain. Subscribe for a new strange question every day.

How it works: the back of your eye, the retina, is lined with light-sensing cells, and whatever sets them off, your brain reads their signal as light. Pressure on the eyeball squeezes the retina and makes its cells fire, much as light does, so you see sparks, blobs and rings with your eyes shut. They are called phosphenes. In the 1660s Isaac Newton tried it with a bodkin, a blunt needle, pushed in beside his own eye, and wrote down the white, dark and coloured circles he saw. Do not copy him. Astronauts see flashes too, in the dark and with their eyes closed, about one every three minutes on the Apollo flights. They are put down to cosmic rays passing through the eye, though exactly how a particle sets the flash off is still debated. The stars from a gentle rub are harmless, but eye doctors advise against rubbing hard or often, and flashes that come by themselves are a reason to see one.
